newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen rebel chief warns of rifts, slams rivals.
newsitem.headline: Chechen rebel chief warns of rifts, slams rivals.

text.p: The presidential election race in Russia's breakaway region of Chechnya is turning bitter as differences grow between leading candidates, regardless of their pledges to keep a united front against Moscow.

Out of 16 candidates only five appear to have a realistic chance, including guerrilla commander Shamil Basayev, acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and Aslan Maskhadov, who recently resigned as head of the interim government.
Basayev on Thursday accused his rivals for the Chechen presidency in elections set for January 27 of turning their backs on the fighters who helped them drive out Russian forces.

The bearded Basayev told a rally in the town of Argun near the capital Grozny that Russia was trying to foment discord among the separatists in a bid to increase its leverage over the breakaway republic.
"Since the end of the war our leaders have pushed away the fighters who won our freedom...If this policy continues it could lead to a rift," he added.

Chechnya's polls campaign -- voters will also elect a parliament -- is now well under way across the tiny, oil-rich territory and the main candidates draw large crowds to their outdoor rallies despite freezing temperatures.
Basayev accused Yandarbiyev and Maskhadov of failing to tackle rising crime and wage and pension arrears.
The election is part of a peace deal agreed with Moscow last August halting 21 months of bloody fighting in which tens of thousands were killed and many more made homeless.

Campaign posters, mostly printed in Turkey and depicting the candidates' faces against the background of Chechnya's green, red and white flag, adorn cars and shop windows and most Chechens questioned by Reuters said they intended to vote.

"We are arguing not about our country's external policy -- all the presidential candidates support Chechen independence -- but about our internal policy," said Basayev, who wore combat fatigues and was accompanied by gun-toting bodyguards.

He accused his rivals of surrounding themselves with supporters of Doku Zavgayev, the former pro-Moscow leader who is widely despised in the mountainous Caucasian region as a traitor to the Chechen cause.

"This policy could lead to war among ourselves because our fighters could explode," he said, speaking in Chechen. "But we are all tired of fighting," he added. Basayev, who hijacked an aircraft to Turkey in 1991, became public enemy number one in Russia after leading a spectacular raid on the southern town of Budennovsk in June 1995.
A group of rebels under his command seized hostages in a hospital and over 100 people were killed.
Basayev was speaking on the first anniversary this week of an ill-fated raid led by another guerrilla leader, Salman Raduyev, in which dozens were killed in the neighbouring region of Dagestan.
At a separate rally in a cemetery where Chechen fighters killed in the raid are buried, Basayev said: "These graves show that our people have truly earned their independence."
"Today we have our freedom but if we fail to use it wisely things will go badly with us," he said.
"Russia hopes we will fight among ourselves and will try to implicate us in its games but it will not succeed."

Under last year's peace deal a decision on Chechnya's final political status was deferred for five years. Moscow hopes to persuade Chechnya to stay within the Russian Federation by providing economic incentives for the war-shattered region.
